t_1: Beep boop! I'm SOL, your space weather robot.
t_2: And I'm Nour, junior astronaut! These space storms really happened.
t_3: Our crews are pretend, but NASA's data is real. Let's keep them safe, CAPCOM!
s_1: This is the real Moon, made from pictures by NASA's LRO spacecraft.
s_2: Zooming to the south pole! NASA picked nine spots here for the next landing.
s_3: Ooh, can we pick a spot with ice? Ice is water!
s_4: Every spot has a catch. Tap a card to look around, then pick one!
s_h_sunny: Sunny ridge. Tons of sunlight for power. But the icy craters are far away.
s_h_crater: Shadowed crater. Ice for science! But less sunlight, so less power.
s_h_plain: Flat plain. Easy landing, short drives. But Earth sits low, so the radio is weak.
s_p_sunny: Sunshine base! Our solar panels will be so happy.
s_p_crater: Ice base! Brrr, but science is cool. Get it? Cool!
s_p_plain: Flat and safe! I hope the radio doesn't crackle.
a_1: Alert! Alert! Real NASA video from the tenth of September, 2017.
a_3: That flash is light. Behind it, a giant cloud blasted out at 2,650 kilometers every second!
a_5: Fast enough to go from Earth to the Moon in under three minutes!
a_6: But the real danger is tiny super-fast particles. That's radiation. NASA saw them arrive just 16 minutes later.
a_7: Sami is out with the rover. Your clock starts now! Watch it, top right.
c1_q: CAPCOM, I found the coolest rock ever! Five more minutes?
c1_home: Aww. Bye bye, rock. Driving home!
c1_ask8: About eight minutes. Nine if Sami sings.
c1_ask6: About six minutes. It's nice and flat out here.
c1_ask_sol: Smart move! Ask first, decide second.
c1_n_say: What if Sami runs home? Running is faster!
c1_n_sol: In a big, heavy spacesuit, over two kilometers? The rover wins!
c1_static: Krrrsh! Static. Earth is low here, so the radio is weak. We lost a minute.
c2_q: The shelter walls are Moon dirt. We can make them thicker. How should we do it?
c2_water: Stacking water bags! Bye bye, plant experiment water.
c2_water_sol: Great shielding! NASA's Orion crew builds a storm shelter from bags of water, food and supplies.
c2_food: Food boxes it is. Careful with the cookies!
c2_food_sol: More stuff around you means more particles get stopped. Food helps a bit.
c2_dirt: Grabbing the digger! I'll pile more Moon dirt on top. I'll be outside for a few minutes.
c2_dirt_sol: Moon dirt is real shielding! NASA says astronauts could pile it over shelters. Just don't get caught outside!
c2_n_say: Let's hide behind the big solar panel tower!
c2_n_sol: Panels are super thin. Particles zip right through. Pick something heavier!
w_out: Come on, Sami! Drive, drive, drive!
w_in: Everyone is in the shelter. Now we wait. Tap the button when you're ready.
w_lina: Lina is still digging outside. Tick tock!
i_out: Uh oh! We're still outside, and my camera is full of white sparkles!
i_in: We're safe inside! The cameras outside are full of white sparkles.
i_r_out: Ouch. Being outside in a particle storm means a big dose.
i_r_none: The shelter walls stopped some, but thicker walls would stop more.
i_r_med: Good job! The extra stuff around the crew blocked more particles.
i_r_strong: Awesome! Thick walls, tiny dose. That's how it's done!
d_lose: Oh no, too much radiation. Let's try again!
d_fact1: Here's what really happened. In 2017, the particles showed up just 16 minutes after the cloud left the Sun. On the Moon, a thick shelter is your best friend.
l2_1: Level two! Real NASA records from May 2024.
l2_2: On the ninth of May, the Sun fired flare after flare. NASA's DONKI lists clouds flying out at over 1,300 kilometers every second.
l2_4: Yep. This storm comes in waves, for days. It's a marathon, not a sprint. Every day in the shelter uses power for air and heat.
l2_c1_q: Nothing has hit us yet. Can we finish fixing the antenna first?
l2_c1_fix: Two more bolts, then we run!
l2_c1_stock: Packing the shelter with food, water and batteries. Long nights ahead!
l2_c1_sol: Checking NASA's DONKI list. I count several fast clouds. Expect more than one wave!
l2_w1: Wave one is here! On Earth, this was the strongest geomagnetic storm in over twenty years.
l2_c2_q: Day two in the shelter. Power is dropping. I can keep the heater or a strong radio link. Not both!
l2_c2_heat: Toasty! But I can barely hear you, CAPCOM.
l2_c2_radio: Radio is crystal clear. Everyone put on an extra sweater!
l2_c2_fix: Heading out to fix the solar tower. Wish me luck!
l2_c2_fix_sol: Risky! More power, but Sami gets a dose out there.
l2_fact: Fun fact! About 90 tiny cosmic particles pass through a space the size of a golf ball every second. A solar storm can add about a thousand more!
l2_c3_q: Day four. It's so quiet now. Can we please go outside?
l2_c3_stay: Checking the data... NASA's records show more fast particles on the thirteenth of May. Good call staying in!
l2_c3_short: Freedom! Just ten minutes, I promise.
l2_w3: Surprise! A second burst of particles, just like NASA saw on the thirteenth of May.
l2_n_say: Let's ask Earth for a weather forecast first!
l2_n_sol: Nice! NASA's space weather team sends forecasts. The forecast says: more storms coming. Stay put!
l2_d_fact: What really happened: In May 2024, Earth had its strongest storm in over twenty years. People saw auroras far from the poles, and NASA found two new temporary radiation belts around Earth. Earth has a magnetic bubble. The Moon doesn't, so shelters matter.
l2_end_win: We survived the big one! High five, CAPCOM!
l2_end_lose: That storm was a monster. Let's try a smarter plan!
hint_idle: Psst! Pick an answer. The clock is ticking!
tap_sami: Hi CAPCOM! Moon rocks are the best rocks.
tap_rover: That's our rover. Its sealed cabin is like a tiny house on wheels.
l3_c3_sol: Real science! NASA grows plants on the Space Station, like chile peppers. Plants need light, and light needs power.
l4_1: Final level! We're going to Mars.
l4_2: In June 2018, a dust storm grew until it covered the whole planet!
l4_3: A dust storm? Is that dangerous?
l4_4: Our Mars base runs on solar panels. No sunlight means no power. And power keeps the air and heat on!
l4_5: Radio takes twelve minutes to reach Mars in this mission. So we write three rules now. Doctor Omar will follow them on his own.
l4_r1_q: Rule one. When the sky gets dark, Omar should...
l4_r2_q: Rule two. When power is short, what gets power first?
l4_r3_q: Rule three. If the battery gets very low, Omar should...
l4_nour_r: I'm writing them in my notebook!
l4_go: Rules sent! They travel to Mars for twelve minutes. Let's watch.
l4_send_q: Want to send Omar a message? It will take twelve minutes to get there.
l4_late: By the time it arrived, Omar had already decided. That's why good rules matter!
l4_safe: The dust is clearing and we still have power. Thanks for the great rules, Earth!
l4_hurt: The power ran out, and the heaters stopped. We had to call for rescue. Next time, better rules.
l4_d_fact: What really happened: NASA's Opportunity rover ran on solar power. It sent its last signal on the tenth of June 2018. NASA listened for months, but the storm had ended its mission. It worked for almost fifteen years, but it was built for just ninety days!
l4_end_win: We did it! Mars crew safe. You're a real CAPCOM!
l4_end_lose: The dark won this time. Let's write smarter rules!
cert: Congratulations, CAPCOM! You kept every crew safe from real space weather. Beep boop, I'm so proud!
t_dose: Quick word! Dose means how much radiation a body soaks up. Low dose, happy crew!
fx_gravity: See the dust float down slowly? The Moon's gravity is only about one sixth of Earth's.
l4_sol: Fun fact! A day on Mars is called a sol. It's about 24 hours and 40 minutes long. Just like my name!
live_1: This is real space weather from NASA's DONKI, from the last month. Live data, straight from the Sun watchers!
live_fail: I can't reach NASA right now, so I won't guess. Try again later!
about_1: Here's every NASA source we used, so you can check our facts.
osdr_l2: Real science from NASA's open data library, OSDR. Scientists study how space radiation can damage cells. That's why we keep the dose low!
l4_d1: Sol one. The sky is turning orange and dim. Following rule one.
l4_d2: Sol two. The Sun is just a fuzzy dot now. Our solar power is dropping.
l4_d3: Sol three. It's dark like night, even at noon! Following rule two.
l4_d4: Sol four. Still dark. Almost no power from the panels.
l4_d5: Sol five. The dust is settling. I can see the Sun again!
l4_sleep: Battery very low! Rule three. Everything is off except the heaters and a clock. We'll wake up to check.
l4_radio: Battery very low! Rule three. The radio stays on to call Earth, but it uses a lot of power.
l4_nuke: Battery very low! Rule three. We're driving to the nuclear rover. It makes power without any sunlight.
l4_curio: Real fact! NASA's Curiosity rover kept working all through this storm. It runs on nuclear power, not sunlight.
rules_1: Quick rules! Keep the dose low, keep the power on, and read each card's cost before you tap!
l3_1: Level three! The twenty-third of July, 2012.
l3_2: NASA's STEREO-A spacecraft watched the Sun throw out one of the fastest clouds ever seen. About three thousand kilometers per second!
l3_3: Look at all those white scratches on the video!
l3_4: Those are fast particles hitting STEREO-A's camera. The cloud went right over it.
l3_5: But which way is it going? Toward our Moon base, or away? You decide what the crew does first.
l3_c1_q: The forecast from Earth is not ready yet. What should the crew do now?
l3_c1_hide: Everybody into the shelter! The greenhouse will have to wait.
l3_c1_ask: Calling Earth for the forecast. The space weather team is on it!
l3_c1_work: We'll keep working, but I'll keep one eye on the sky.
l3_map: The forecast is here! This is NASA's real computer model of the cloud. The Sun is in the middle. The red is the cloud.
l3_c2_q: Find the little blue Earth near the bottom. Our Moon is right next to it. Is the red cloud coming to us?
l3_c2_away: Right! The cloud is going the other way, toward STEREO-A. Back to work!
l3_c2_hide: Hmm, the cloud was going the other way. Hiding cost power and time for nothing.
l3_n_say: SOL, how do I read this map?
l3_n_sol: Find the blue Earth dot. Then see where the red cloud is pointing. Red near Earth means trouble. Red far away means we're okay!
l3_c3_q: It's harvest week in the greenhouse! The plant lamps need power. How bright?
l3_c3_full: Full lamps! Big, crunchy lettuce for everyone.
l3_c3_half: Half lamps. Smaller crops, but we save power.
l3_c3_off: Lamps off. The plants will droop, and we'll eat stored food.
l3_whatif: Now, a what if! NASA scientists said: if this cloud had left one week earlier, Earth would have been in its path.
l3_whatif2: Let's practice. Imagine it's aimed at our Moon base. Fast particles could arrive in minutes! Quick, build the shelter!
l3_w_water: Water bags stacked! Water is great at stopping particles.
l3_w_food: Food boxes stacked. Not as thick, but it helps.
l3_w_dirt: I'm shoveling Moon dirt on the roof. Hurry, hurry!
l3_w_none: It missed us last time. It'll miss us again, right?
l3_i_ok: The pretend storm hits. Good walls! The crew is okay.
l3_i_bad: The pretend storm hits. Ouch! Too many particles got through.
l3_end_win: Great forecasting, CAPCOM! You didn't panic, and you were ready.
l3_end_lose: Forecasts are tricky. Let's try again!
l3_d_fact: What really happened: the July 2012 cloud missed Earth and the Moon. NASA scientists said it was at least as strong as the biggest storm ever recorded, back in 1859. That's why NASA watches the Sun every day.
